title: Handling Outliers
subtopics: Distinguishing errors from genuine rare events
learning_outcomes: Explain handling outliers and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of handling outliers to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study handling outliers in the context of data cleaning and preprocessing. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Handling Outliers matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Cleaning means making explicit, documented decisions about quality problems while preserving provenance and avoiding transformations that leak future information.

items.title: Detecting unusual values
items.text: Define detecting unusual values in relation to handling outliers; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: IQR and z-score methods
items.text: Work through iqr and z-score methods using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Domain-based validation
items.text: Check the edge cases for domain-based validation: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Capping, transforming, or retaining outliers
items.text: Document the rule or choice for capping, transforming, or retaining outliers so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by handling outliers. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Dropping missing values changes the analyzed sample; document the choice.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.
